catalog_quote: There are three underlying level tones in Gaahmg illustrated by the words of table 5. ... Rising and falling tone is analyzed as a sequence of two level tones. The level tones combine and result in nine tone melodies which are all contrastive in the same monosyllabic syllable type—three level, three falling, and three rising. The same, as well as additional tone melodies, are contrastive in disyllabic syllable patterns. Unlike some African tone languages, tone is not affected by consonants, tone is stable—it does not shift from one syllable to another, and tone does not down-step or down-drift. The functional load of tone is very high, both in the distinction of words and in the expression of grammatical functions. The tone bearing unit is the syllable. In roots with fewer tones than the number of syllables, such as in three-syllable nouns with two tones, tone is assigned right-to-left,…
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title (Pitts 2009, Dye 1974) are psychological-stress papers, irrelevant, and are not even among the 46 Glottolog references for gaam1241; nothing else with a stress/accent title exists for Gaahmg (Crossref 'Gaahmg' gives 4 works, none on stress). The catalog's deciding source, Stirtz 2012 (open LOT PDF, now, was re-read: its section 2.4 (pp. 43-44) confirms the 'tonal' coding (three level tones, nine melodies, TBU = syllable, no downstep) and the entire grammar never uses the word 'stress' or 'accent'. Trommer 2025 (PDA, held by the project) is likewise silent on stress. WALS codes Ingessana only for Tone (13A simple tone system, after Crewe 1975) with no stress datapoints. Unread print-only candidates: Crewe 1975 (medium priority) and Stirtz 2004 (low). No new statement supersedes the catalog source.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim at Stirtz 2012 section 2.4, pp.43-44 of the LOT 296 text we hold; the 'zero hits for stress/accent/prominence/intonation' claim in the locator re-verified by a full-text search for stress/accent. (2) Deciding source is a 350-pp modern reference grammar (Leiden PhD 2012 / LOT 2011) by the field linguist who produced essentially all modern Gaahmg documentation; Glottolog lists nothing larger or newer, and Trommer 2025 (PDA, downloaded now, open access) states it is the only detailed description and builds a full tonal analysis on it with syllable TBU and no metrical structure, confirming the 'tonal, no word stress stated' coding. (3) Unheld items are an 18-pp 2004 paper by the same author, a 21-pp 1975 Khartoum pamphlet and an unpublished 1999 SIL write-up; none is likely to change the classification, listed low priority for completeness. No JIPA Illustration or instrumental prosody study was found via Crossr

sources.note: The whole 350-page grammar's text layer contains no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominen'; word stress is never mentioned. Section 2.4 Tone (pp. 43-44) describes three underlying level tones H/M/L, nine contrastive melodies on one syllable type, TBU = syllable, tone stable (no shifting, no downstep/downdrift), very high functional load; tone assignment in roots is right-to-left regardless of syllable weight. Confirms the catalog's classification 'tonal' and shows the source is silent on any stress system.

sources.quote: p.4: 'The only detailed description of the language is the recent grammar by Stirtz (2011), which is also the source of all data discussed in this paper.' p.5: 'In the description given by Stirtz (2011:44), Gaahmg has three contrastive level tones H(igh), M(id), and L(ow) ... H, M and L can in principle be freely combined to form two-tone and three-tone contours on single syllables'. p.10: 'With Stirtz (2011) I assume that the syllable is in all cases the TBU.' A 65-page formal tone analysis; a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|metrical|foot = zero hits. No stress or accent is posited anywhere.
sources.locator: sec. 2.1 pp.4-5; sec. 3 p.10 (the text layer)
sources.note: Tonal morphology (Gestalt contours, register-tier analysis) built on Stirtz's data; the text contains no occurrence of stress/accent/metrical/foot. Silent on word stress; consistent with a purely tonal system.
